rw: Regular audits catch errors, bias and harmful outcomes that creep in as data, users and conditions change, which makes ongoing checks of a deployed AI system worthwhile.

ww.To remove the need for rules and for hum: Audits add oversight rather than replace it, so removing rules and human review of results would raise risk and is the opposite of what an audit is for.
ww.To make the system more costly, since ea: Expense is a side effect of auditing, never its goal, and a reason that aims at higher cost is not a sound justification for checking an AI system.
ww.To keep users from seeing results of the: Audits examine whether the system behaves well and fairly, so hiding its results from users would reduce transparency and does nothing to find problems in its work.

rw: Responsible AI means designing and using systems that are safe, fair and accountable, so that people can trust them and someone answers for the harms they may cause.

ww.Building AI as fast as possible without: Skipping all testing makes AI unsafe and unreliable, so building as fast as possible without testing is the opposite of responsible practice and invites harm to users.
ww.Using AI only to cut costs and to reduce: Responsible AI is about safe, fair and accountable outcomes for people, and focusing only on cutting costs or staff ignores those duties and the people affected by decisions.
ww.Hiding AI use from regulators and from t: Hiding AI use from regulators and the public removes transparency and accountability, which are core parts of responsible AI, so it describes irresponsible behavior instead.

rw: Data literacy is the ability to read, understand and question data and the conclusions drawn from it, which lets people spot weak evidence and misleading claims.

ww.Being able to type very fast and to writ: Typing speed and report length have nothing to do with data skills, and error-free writing says nothing about whether someone can interpret or question numbers and charts.
ww.Being able to memorize large tables of n: Memorizing large tables is not data literacy, since the skill is understanding and judging data, and recalling numbers from memory does not show that anyone grasps their meaning.
ww.Being able to buy data cheaply from sell: Buying data cheaply is a commercial skill and says nothing about understanding it, so purchasing ability does not make a person able to read or question data.

rw: Starting the vertical axis at 90 instead of 0 makes a small gap look large, which distorts the picture and so makes this chart a misleading visualization.

ww.A data cleaning step done: Data cleaning means fixing errors, duplicates or missing values in the data itself, while changing where an axis starts only alters how the chart looks to viewers.
ww.A way to protect privacy: Privacy protection involves masking or removing personal details, and a truncated axis hides nothing about individuals, so it has no connection to protecting anyone's data.
ww.A fair chart of the data: A fair chart shows differences at honest scale, usually with the axis starting at zero for bars, so a chart exaggerating a small gap is not fair.

rw: A data-driven decision relies on analysis of relevant data to guide the choice, which reduces guesswork and lets the reasoning be checked by others afterward.

ww.A choice made by the loudest voice in th: A decision driven by the loudest voice rests on influence and not evidence, so it is not based on analysis of data and does not qualify as data-driven.
ww.A choice made without any information, b: A choice made with no information is a guess by definition, and data-driven decisions are the opposite because they depend on evidence gathered and analyzed first.
ww.A choice made by flipping a coin in the: Flipping a coin is pure chance and uses no data at all, so it cannot be called a decision based on analysis of evidence.

rw: An analyst should test for confounders such as seasons, promotions or price changes that could also explain the rise before claiming that the ad caused higher sales.

ww.Nothing, because timing proves cause and: Timing alone does not prove cause, because events can follow each other by coincidence, so concluding the ad worked without any further checks is a classic correlation error.
ww.Only the manager's opinion about the ad: Relying only on the manager's opinion repeats the unsupported claim and checks no data, so it cannot tell whether the ad or something else drove the increase.
ww.Only the color of the ad and the font th: The ad's color and font do not explain a sales rise on their own, and checking only them ignores outside factors that could account for the change.

rw: The median is the middle value once the data are sorted, with half the values below it and half above, which makes it a resistant measure of center.

ww.The spread of the data around a mean: The spread of data around a mean describes variation, such as standard deviation, and not the median, which is a measure of the center of the data.
ww.The average of all of the data values: The average of all values is the mean, found by adding them and dividing by the count, and is a different measure from the median.
ww.The value that appears most often here: The value that appears most often is the mode, which can differ from the median, so this describes a different measure of center.

rw: With one extreme value of 500, the median of 30, 32, 35, 36 and 500 is 35, which stays close to most incomes and so represents a typical person best.

ww.The maximum: The maximum is 500, which is far above the other four incomes, so it describes only the single extreme value and not a typical income in the town.
ww.The mean: The mean is (30+32+35+36+500)/5 = 633/5 = 126.6, which is pulled far above four of the five incomes by the outlier and so misleads here.
ww.The range: The range is 500 - 30 = 470, which measures spread and not a typical income, so it cannot represent what a typical person in the town earns.

rw: Standard deviation measures how spread out values are around the mean, so a larger value means the data are more scattered and a smaller one means they cluster closely.

ww.The average of the values, found by addi: Adding values and dividing by their count gives the mean, which measures the center of the data, whereas standard deviation measures how far values spread from that center.
ww.The count of values in a data set that a: Counting the values above the mean is a simple tally and says nothing about how far values lie from the mean, which is what standard deviation measures.
ww.The middle of the data after it is sorte: The middle of sorted data is the median, a measure of center, so it describes a different statistic from standard deviation, which measures spread.

rw: With equal means, the smaller standard deviation signals less spread, and Class A at 2 is far tighter than Class B at 15, so Class A is more consistent.

ww.Class B: Class B has a standard deviation of 15, much larger than 2, so its scores are more scattered around the shared mean and it is less consistent.
ww.No mean: Both classes do have a mean, since the question says they share one, so the claim of no mean is false and answers nothing about consistency.
ww.Identical: The classes share a mean but differ in spread, 2 versus 15, so their score patterns are not identical and consistency clearly differs between them.

rw: The empirical rule says about 68% of values in a normal distribution fall within one standard deviation of the mean, with 95% within two and 99.7% within three.

ww.About 99.7%: About 99.7% of values lie within three standard deviations of the mean, not one, so this figure belongs to a much wider interval than the one asked about.
ww.About 50%: Fifty percent is the share below the mean in a symmetric distribution and not the share within one standard deviation, which is about 68% in a normal distribution.
ww.About 10%: Ten percent is far too small, since the central region within one standard deviation holds about 68% of a normal distribution, which is most of the values.

rw: A population is the entire group of interest, while a sample is a smaller subset drawn from it and used to learn about the whole group.

ww.Two names for the same thing in the fiel: Population and sample are different ideas, since a sample is only part of the population, so calling them two names for one thing is wrong in statistics.
ww.A graph versus a table of data in a repo: Population and sample describe groups of subjects or items being studied, not display formats, so comparing them to a graph and a table confuses data with its presentation.
ww.A subset versus the full group, where th: This reverses the definitions, because a sample is the smaller subset and the population is the full group, so the sample cannot be the larger of the two.

rw: Sampling bias happens when the way a sample is chosen systematically leaves out or overweights some groups, so results do not represent the whole population.

ww.A random sample drawn from every member: A random sample drawn from every member gives each person a fair chance, which reduces bias, so this describes a sound method and not sampling bias.
ww.A sample with no data in it, so that not: An empty sample has no data and so cannot be measured, but sampling bias concerns samples that exist yet misrepresent the population, so this does not fit.
ww.A very large sample that includes thousa: Large size does not cure bias, since a huge sample from the wrong group still misleads, and size alone is not what sampling bias means.

rw: Surveying only students in the cafeteria line leaves out those who bring lunch or skip it, so the sample misrepresents all students, which is sampling bias.

ww.Many variables: Many variables is not the issue here, since the flaw lies in who was asked and not in how many measures were collected in the survey.
ww.Pure randomness: The choice of only cafeteria-line students is not random, since it follows a clear pattern of who is included, so pure randomness does not describe the problem.
ww.No problem at all: Asking only one group leaves out students who may feel differently about lunches, so there is a real problem, and saying there is none ignores the bias created.

rw: The two rise together, which is a correlation, and a shared cause such as hot weather explains both, so correlation here does not mean one causes the other.

ww.Sunburn causes ice cream sales, because: Sunburn does not cause ice cream sales, because both simply rise with summer heat, and burned people buying a cold treat is an unsupported story about cause.
ww.Ice cream causes sunburn because of the: Ice cream does not cause sunburn, since sunburn comes from sun exposure, and the sugar and cold in the treat have no effect on skin damage.
ww.They are unrelated, since the two have n: The data show both rising in summer, so they are related in a measurable way, and calling them unrelated ignores the correlation that the numbers show.

rw: Conditional probability is the chance of an event given that another event has already occurred, written P(A given B), and it changes how likely A is judged to be.

ww.A random guess made by an analyst with n: A random guess with no data is not a probability calculation, and conditional probability is a precise measure that depends on a stated known event.
ww.The chance an event never happens, howev: An event that never happens has probability zero, which is a fixed value and not conditional probability, which depends on another event having occurred.
ww.The sum of all probabilities in a sample: All probabilities across a sample space add to 1, which is a rule about totals and does not define the chance of one event given another.

rw: A fair die has 3 even faces out of 6, namely 2, 4 and 6, so the probability of rolling an even number is 3/6 = 1/2.

ww.1/6: One in six is the chance of a single specific face, but there are 3 even faces, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2 and not 1/6.
ww.1/3: One third would match only 2 favorable faces out of 6, but the even faces are 2, 4 and 6, which makes 3 of 6 or 1/2.
ww.2/3: Two thirds would need 4 favorable faces out of 6, but only 3 faces are even, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2 and not 2/3.

rw: A p-value is the probability of seeing results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis is true, so small values count as evidence against it.

ww.The size of the sample used in the test,: Sample size is the count of observations in the test, which is a separate quantity from a p-value, which measures how surprising the results would be under the null.
ww.The mean of the data, found by adding al: The mean is found by adding values and dividing by their count and describes the center of the data, not the evidence against a null hypothesis.
ww.The probability the null hypothesis is t: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, which is a common misreading, because it assumes the null is true and asks about the data.

rw: A hypothesis test weighs how well sample data support or contradict a claim about a population, deciding whether the evidence is strong enough to doubt the claim.

ww.Cleaning missing values from a data set: Cleaning missing values is data preparation done before analysis, and it does not test any claim about a population or weigh evidence against a stated hypothesis.
ww.Drawing charts only, to show the results: Drawing charts only displays results and does not weigh evidence about a claim, so it is not what a hypothesis test is used for.
ww.Collecting data without a plan, to see w: Collecting data with no plan is aimless exploration, whereas a hypothesis test starts with a stated claim and uses data to check it against a standard.

rw: Removing the duplicate record keeps one entry per customer and stops that customer from being counted twice, which is the standard cleaning step for repeated rows.

ww.Delete the whole data table: Deleting the whole table would destroy all the valid records along with the repeat, which is far too drastic when only one repeated entry needs fixing.
ww.Ignore it completely for now: Ignoring a duplicate leaves the same customer counted twice, which inflates totals and skews results, so the problem should be fixed and not left in place.
ww.Double every value in the set: Doubling every value would distort the whole data set and make totals wrong, and it does nothing to fix the single customer listed twice.

rw: A scatter plot places each observation as a point by its two values, so patterns such as trends, clusters and correlation between the variables become visible.

ww.A word cloud: A word cloud shows how often words appear in text, so it cannot display how two numeric variables relate to each other.
ww.A bar chart: A bar chart compares values across categories, which does not show how two numeric variables move together, so it is the wrong tool for this question.
ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows parts of one whole, so it cannot display a relationship between two numeric variables across many observations.

rw: A histogram groups one numeric variable into bins and shows how many values fall in each, which displays the shape of its distribution.

ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows shares of a whole across categories, so it cannot show how the values of a numeric variable are spread across a range.
ww.A scatter plot: A scatter plot shows the relation between two variables, so it does not display the distribution of a single numeric variable.
ww.A line chart: A line chart usually tracks values over time or an ordered sequence, and it does not group a numeric variable into bins to show its distribution.

rw: A data dictionary describes each field in a data set, including its name, type, meaning and allowed values, so that users read and use the data correctly.

ww.A backup of the data kept on a safe serv: A backup is a stored copy kept for recovery, which protects the data but does not explain what each field in the data set means.
ww.A list of English words with their meani: An English dictionary lists general words and meanings, while a data dictionary documents the specific fields of one data set, so the two serve different purposes.
ww.A chart of the data shown as a set of ba: A chart of bars displays values visually, but a data dictionary is a text description of fields and not a graph of the data.

rw: Normalization rescales values to a common range or organizes data into a consistent structure, so that features or tables can be compared and used together.

ww.Hiding columns from view in a table or s: Hiding columns only changes what is visible in a table and leaves the values and their scale unchanged, so it is not normalization.
ww.Deleting all values from the data set at: Deleting all values removes the data entirely, which defeats the purpose, since normalization changes scale or structure while keeping the information that the data contain.
ww.Randomly shuffling rows so the record or: Shuffling rows only changes their order and leaves every value untouched, so it does not rescale the data or give it a common structure.

rw: Incomes in dollars are numerically far larger than heights in centimeters, so unscaled they can dominate distance-based models, and scaling lets each feature contribute fairly.

ww.To make the data secret from all others: Scaling is a technical step and does not hide anything, so keeping data secret from others is not the reason for putting heights and incomes on one scale.
ww.To remove all variation from the data se: Scaling keeps the differences between values and just changes their units, so it does not remove variation, and a model still needs that variation to learn.
ww.To change the data's meaning for analyst: Scaling puts features on similar ranges without changing what the data mean, so the claim that it alters meaning for analysts is wrong.

rw: Mean imputation fills missing values with the average of the observed values in that column, which keeps the row in the data instead of dropping it.

ww.Data encryption: Encryption protects data by scrambling it and has nothing to do with filling gaps, so it is not the name for replacing missing values with an average.
ww.Feature scaling: Feature scaling changes the range of values and does not fill in empty cells, so it is a different step from imputing missing data.
ww.Outlier removal: Outlier removal deletes extreme values, but filling gaps with the average adds values instead of removing them, so the two steps are not the same.

rw: SQL is a language for querying and managing data stored in relational databases, letting users select, filter, join and update rows in tables.

ww.Writing music for songs and films in a s: Writing music is a creative task done with audio software, and SQL is a database language with no role in composing songs or film scores.
ww.Editing video clips for films and online: Video editing needs software for cutting and arranging footage, while SQL works with tables of data and cannot edit clips or posts.
ww.Designing logos and brand marks for new: Logo design is a visual art done with graphics tools, whereas SQL is used for working with stored data and is not a design tool.

rw: WHERE sets a condition that each row must meet, so only matching rows are returned, which makes it the SQL clause that filters rows.

ww.ORDER BY: ORDER BY sorts the rows of a result into a chosen order, but it does not remove any rows, so it does not filter them.
ww.SELECT: SELECT chooses which columns appear in the output, and it does not decide which rows are kept, so it is not the filtering clause.
ww.FROM: FROM names the table or tables the data come from and does not apply a condition to rows, so it does not filter them.

rw: Python is widely used in data science for analysis, visualization and building models, thanks to libraries such as pandas, matplotlib and scikit-learn.

ww.Driving cars manually on roads to collec: Python is a programming language and cannot drive a car by hand, so manual driving to collect data is not a use of Python.
ww.Painting walls in homes and offices by h: Painting walls is manual work with no link to programming, so it is not something Python is used for in data science.
ww.Cooking recipes for meals in a home kitc: Cooking meals in a kitchen has no connection to Python, which is a programming language used for data work and not for preparing food.

rw: A pivot table summarizes and groups data by categories, letting users total, count or average values by region, product or date without writing formulas.

ww.Writing programs in code for use on a co: Writing programs is done in code editors, while a pivot table summarizes data in a sheet and does not create software for a computer.
ww.Sending email messages to clients and st: Email is sent through mail software, and a pivot table does not send messages to clients or staff, since its job is to summarize data.
ww.Drawing images and sketches by hand on p: Drawing by hand on paper is unrelated to spreadsheets, so it is not the purpose of a pivot table, which works on rows of data.

rw: A pivot table groups rows by region and sums the sales for each in a few clicks, which makes it the quickest tool for this question.

ww.A word processor: A word processor is built for writing documents and does not total values by group, so it would be slow and awkward for this task.
ww.A calendar: A calendar organizes dates and events and cannot summarize numbers by region, so it is the wrong tool for finding total sales.
ww.A photo editor: A photo editor changes images and cannot add up sales figures from a table, so it is unsuited to totaling sales by region.

rw: A data pipeline is a set of automated steps that extract, move and transform data from a source to a destination, so it arrives ready for use.

ww.A password manager that stores and fills: A password manager stores and fills in logins, which is a security tool and not a series of steps that moves and changes data.
ww.A water pipe for servers that carries co: A water pipe carrying coolant is physical cooling equipment, and a data pipeline is software that moves data, so the name is only a loose metaphor.
ww.A single chart that shows one set of num: A single chart shows one set of numbers and does not move or transform data between systems, so it is not a data pipeline.

rw: Artificial intelligence means computer systems that perform tasks that usually require human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images, learning from data and making decisions.

ww.A database of facts that people can sear: A database of facts stores information that people look up, but it does not perform tasks needing intelligence, so it is not artificial intelligence itself.
ww.A robot with a metal body only, which ca: AI does not need a metal body, since most AI is software with no physical form, so limiting it to walking robots is far too narrow.
ww.Any machine with a screen that displays: A machine with a screen only displays content, and having a display says nothing about performing tasks that need human-like intelligence, so it does not define AI.

rw: Studying thousands of labeled emails to learn which are spam is supervised machine learning, because the labels guide the model toward the right answers.

ww.Manual rule writing only: The filter improves by learning from examples and does not rely on rules written by hand, so manual rule writing alone does not describe the process.
ww.Unsupervised clustering: Unsupervised clustering finds groups in data with no labels, but these emails are labeled spam or not spam, so this is not unsupervised.
ww.Data deletion steps only: Deleting data does not teach a filter anything, whereas the filter improves by learning from labeled examples, so this does not describe what is happening.

rw: Grouping customers by similar buying habits with no predefined categories or labels is unsupervised learning, specifically clustering, since the algorithm finds the groups on its own.

ww.Manual sorting of the customer lists: Sorting by hand means a person sets the groups, but here the store finds groups itself from buying habits, so this is not manual sorting.
ww.Reinforcement learning methods: Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards and penalties from actions, which does not match grouping customers by their buying habits.
ww.Supervised classification only: Supervised classification needs labeled categories set in advance, but the scenario says there are none, so supervised classification does not apply.

rw: Recognizing objects in images is a classic deep learning task, because neural networks with many layers learn visual features directly from large sets of pictures.

ww.Sorting a short list of names: Sorting a short list of names is a simple routine solved by a standard algorithm, so it needs no deep learning.
ww.Adding two numbers together: Adding two numbers is basic arithmetic with fixed rules, so it requires no neural network and is not tied to deep learning.
ww.Storing a file on a hard disk: Storing a file is a function of the operating system and disk, and it involves no learning of patterns from data.

rw: Training data is the set of examples used to teach a model patterns, so it can later make predictions on new inputs.

ww.Data kept secret from the model: Training data is given to the model so it can learn from it, which is the opposite of keeping the data secret from the model.
ww.Data used only after deployment: Data used only after deployment would be live input and not training data, because training happens before deployment to teach the model.
ww.Data that is deleted after each use: Deleting data after each use does not describe training data, which is kept and used repeatedly so the model learns from it.

rw: Test data is held back from training and used to measure how well the trained model performs on examples it has not seen.

ww.Cleaning the model by removing old code: Cleaning code and files is housekeeping and has nothing to do with evaluating a model, which is what test data is for.
ww.Hiding errors in the results so that nob: Test data is meant to reveal errors honestly, so hiding errors from others would defeat its purpose of showing true performance.
ww.Training the model on the examples it wi: Training is done with the training set, and test data is kept separate so that it can check the model on new examples.

rw: Scoring 99% on training data but 60% on new data shows the model memorized the training set and fails to generalize, which is overfitting.

ww.Great fit: A great fit would score well on both training and new data, but a drop from 99% to 60% shows the opposite, so this is not a great fit.
ww.A faster PC: A faster computer changes how quickly a model runs and does not explain a large gap between training and new data scores.
ww.Underfitting: Underfitting gives poor scores on training data too, but this model scores 99% on training data, so it does not fit the pattern described.

rw: Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the pattern in the data, so it performs poorly on both training data and new data.

ww.A model that memorizes noise in the trai: Memorizing noise in training data is overfitting, which is the opposite problem, since an underfit model is too simple and misses the real pattern.
ww.A model with extra features that it does: Extra unneeded features tend to add complexity and risk overfitting, whereas underfitting comes from a model that is too simple to capture the pattern.
ww.A model that is accurate on training dat: A model accurate on both training and new data fits well, so it is a good result and not underfitting.

rw: More training data helps a model learn general patterns and a simpler model has less capacity to memorize noise, so both reduce overfitting.

ww.Remove the test set from the data entire: The test set is needed to measure generalization honestly, so removing it hides overfitting instead of reducing it.
ww.Add noise labels to the training data se: Adding noisy labels makes the training data worse and tends to push a model to memorize errors, which raises overfitting.
ww.Memorize the training set so the model i: Memorizing the training set is overfitting itself, and it makes the model fail on new data, so it cannot help reduce it.

rw: A feature is an input variable, such as size or age, that a model uses to make predictions, and a model typically takes several of them.

ww.A bug in the code that makes the program: A bug stops a program from working correctly, but a feature in machine learning is an input used for prediction, so the two are unrelated.
ww.A chart title shown above the graph in a: A chart title labels a graph, but a feature in machine learning is a data input, so a title is not what the word means here.
ww.The model's final answer, shown to the u: The model's final answer is its output or prediction, which is different from a feature, since features are the inputs that the model uses.

rw: A label is the correct output for a training example, such as spam or not spam, which the model learns to predict from the features.

ww.A column name only, shown at the top: A column name is a header, but a label in machine learning is the answer to be predicted, so a name shown at the top is not the meaning.
ww.A chart legend that explains colors in a: A chart legend explains colors on a graph, which is a plotting term, and a label in machine learning is the known output for an example.
ww.A random number picked by the computer: A label is not random and is set by the data, so a random number picked by the computer does not describe it.

rw: The house price is what the model is trying to predict from size and location, so it is the label, or target, of this problem.

ww.The size in feet: The size in feet is an input used to predict price, which makes it a feature and not the label that the model predicts.
ww.The location: The location is also an input used to predict the price, so it is a feature, and the label is the output being predicted.
ww.The seller's name: The seller's name is not part of the problem and does not help predict price, and it is neither the target nor a useful feature.

rw: Classification is a supervised task that predicts which category an item belongs to, such as spam or not spam, or which type of flower a photo shows.

ww.Removing data from a table or a file on: Removing data from a table is a data editing step and does not assign items to categories, which is what classification does.
ww.Grouping data without labels into cluste: Grouping data without labels into clusters is unsupervised clustering, whereas classification uses known labeled categories to predict the class of a new item.
ww.Predicting a number, such as a house pri: Predicting a number, such as a house price, is regression, not classification, which instead predicts a category label.

rw: Regression predicts a numeric value, such as price, temperature or sales, from input features, which separates it from classification that predicts categories.

ww.Grouping items into categories: Grouping items into categories describes classification or clustering, whereas regression predicts a numeric value from input features.
ww.Storing data on a disk: Storing data on a disk is a storage function with no learning or prediction involved, so it is not regression.
ww.Predicting a category label: Predicting a category label is classification, and regression is the other main supervised task, which predicts a number.

rw: Predicting tomorrow's temperature means estimating a numeric value, which is regression, since the output is a number on a continuous scale.

ww.Encryption: Encryption scrambles data to protect it and is not a type of prediction task, so it does not describe forecasting a temperature.
ww.Classification: Classification predicts a category, but tomorrow's temperature is a number on a continuous scale, so it is not a classification task.
ww.Clustering: Clustering groups similar items without labels and does not predict a specific number, so it does not match forecasting a temperature.

rw: Accuracy is the share of predictions that are correct, found by dividing correct predictions by the total number of predictions made.

ww.The speed of a model on the hardware: The speed of a model on hardware is its performance in time, not accuracy, which measures how often predictions are right.
ww.The size of a model file on a hard disk: The size of a model file measures storage, which has nothing to do with how often predictions are correct, which is accuracy.
ww.The cost of training a model on servers: The cost of training is a resource measure and not a measure of correctness, so it does not define accuracy.

rw: The model never flags a single fraud case, so it is useless for its real purpose even though 99 of every 100 transactions are legitimate, which gives the high score.

ww.Accuracy is always perfect: Accuracy is not always perfect, since this model gets 99% only because fraud is rare, and it misses every fraud case, so the claim is false.
ww.It catches all of the fraud: The model always says not fraud, so it catches none of the fraud and does not catch all of it, which is the reverse of the facts.
ww.It uses far too much data: The amount of data used is not the issue, since the 99% comes from class imbalance, with fraud being only 1% of cases, and not from data quantity.

rw: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are right, and recall is the share of actual positives the model finds, so they show different kinds of error.

ww.Training time and storage, the two measu: Training time and storage are resource measures, whereas precision and recall measure the quality of a model's positive predictions, so this answer describes something different.
ww.Size and color of data, the two properti: Size and color of data describe how data or a chart looks and say nothing about prediction quality, which is what precision and recall measure.
ww.Speed and cost of a model, the two measu: Speed and cost describe how a model runs and what it costs, while precision and recall measure how correct its positive predictions are and how many positives it finds.

rw: The model learned the imbalance in past hiring from its training data and reproduces it, which is bias inherited from training data.

ww.Random noise in the whole data: The bias follows a clear pattern in favor of men, so it is systematic and not random noise, since noise would not favor one group.
ww.Perfect fairness, as past hires show: Favoring men because past hires were mostly men repeats historical imbalance and is not fair, so calling it perfect fairness is wrong.
ww.Hardware failure in a data server: Hardware failure would cause crashes or corrupted outputs and not a consistent preference for one gender, so it cannot explain the pattern.

rw: Anonymization removes or masks personal identifiers such as names and ID numbers so that individuals cannot easily be identified from the data.

ww.Deleting the analysis once the project h: Deleting the analysis removes work results and does nothing to protect personal identities in the data, so it is not anonymization.
ww.Selling data to anyone who asks, names l: Selling data to anyone who asks is a privacy risk, and leaving names out does not make a sale responsible or define anonymization.
ww.Adding names to data records to track ea: Adding names makes records easier to trace back to individuals, which is the opposite of anonymization, so it increases privacy risk.

rw: Informed consent means people understand how their data will be used and freely agree to it before it is collected.

ww.Data is collected by default always, wit: Collecting data by default with no choice removes the person's say, so it is not informed consent, which requires a real option.
ww.Data is sold in secret to firms that pay: Selling data in secret means people are unaware of its use, so there is no informed consent, since consent requires knowing what happens.
ww.Data is taken without telling people, th: Taking data without telling people and using it as one likes gives them no knowledge or choice, so it violates informed consent.

rw: Collecting location data without telling users breaks transparency and consent, since people have a right to know what is gathered and agree to it.

ww.Accuracy of data and updates: Accuracy and updates concern data quality, but the problem here is that users were never told about collection, which breaks a different principle.
ww.Backup policy for the files: A backup policy concerns data protection against loss and has no bearing on whether users were told about the location data collection.
ww.Data compression of files: Data compression reduces file size and has nothing to do with informing users, so it is not the principle violated by secret collection.

rw: Human oversight lets people catch errors and bias in high-stakes decisions such as loans and keeps someone accountable for outcomes that affect lives.

ww.To remove all automation from the proces: Human oversight does not aim to remove all automation, since automation still brings benefits, and the goal is to add review where decisions are high-stakes.
ww.To make the AI slower for no reason at a: Oversight is not meant to slow the AI for no reason, and any added review step exists to catch mistakes in decisions that affect people.
ww.To hide the process from the public and: Hiding the process would reduce transparency and trust, but oversight adds checks on loans and similar decisions, so concealment is not its purpose.

rw: A misleading graph distorts the data it shows, for example by cutting off the axis so differences look larger than they are.

ww.A chart with accurate scales showing the: A chart with accurate scales and real values represents the data honestly, which makes it a fair graph and not a misleading one.
ww.A chart with a title placed above the gr: A title above a graph is a normal feature that helps readers, and placing it there does not distort the data in any way.
ww.A chart with clear labels on both of its: Clear labels on both axes and a title help readers understand the chart, so they make it more honest and not misleading.

rw: A truncated axis starts above zero, which cuts off the base of the bars and exaggerates differences, so a small gap looks huge to viewers.

ww.A correct and honest scale, showing real: Starting the axis at 95 hides most of the bar's height, so the scale is not honest, and a small gap is made to look large.
ww.A normal distribution of the data values: A normal distribution describes the shape of data values and not how an axis is drawn, so it is unrelated to the scale problem.
ww.A log scale that grows by powers of ten: A log scale grows by powers of ten and has an evenly spaced multiplicative axis, whereas this axis simply starts at 95 and cuts the bars.

rw: Data provenance is the record of where data came from and how it has changed along the way, which supports trust and traceability.

ww.The color of a chart that is used to sho: The color of a chart is a design choice and says nothing about where data came from, which is what provenance records.
ww.The speed of a query that runs on a data: Query speed measures performance of a database server and has nothing to do with the origin or history of the data.
ww.The size of a file that is stored on a h: File size is a storage measure and does not tell where data originated or what was done to it.

rw: The source affects how reliable the data are, what biases they may carry and whether they suit the intended use, so it matters to analysts.

ww.Only the file name matters, as a title i: A file name tells nothing about quality, so judging a data set only by its title ignores where it came from and how it was gathered.
ww.Only the file size matters to most analy: File size says nothing about reliability or bias, so basing a judgment on size alone ignores the source, which is what matters.
ww.It never matters to any analyst or any u: The source often decides how far data can be trusted, so claiming it never matters to anyone ignores a main factor in data quality.

rw: A dataset is a structured collection of data, often arranged in rows for records and columns for variables, ready for analysis.

ww.A type of chart that shows values as bar: A chart displays data and is not the data itself, so it is not a dataset, which is the underlying collection of values.
ww.A single number that sums up the data, s: A single number such as a mean or total summarizes data and is not a collection of records, so it does not define a dataset.
ww.A computer program that processes data i: A program that processes data is software, whereas a dataset is the data it works on, so these are different things.

rw: In a table each row usually holds one record, also called an observation, such as one customer or one sale, with a value per column.

ww.A variable or column: A variable or column runs vertically down the table and holds one attribute for every record, so it is not a row.
ww.A formula in a cell: A formula in a cell is a calculation in a spreadsheet, which is different from a row, a full line of values for one record.
ww.A header at the top: A header sits at the top and names the columns, so it is a label for the data and not a row of records.

rw: A column usually holds one variable, also called a field, such as age or city, with one value for every record in the table.

ww.An observation or row: An observation, or row, runs across the table, whereas a column runs down it, so this describes a row and not a column.
ww.A database table: A database table is the whole structure holding many rows and columns, so a single column is only a part of a table.
ww.A record or a row: A record or row runs across the table, so it is the other dimension, and a column is not called a record.

rw: Structured data is organized in a fixed format, such as rows and columns in a table, which makes it easy to search and analyze.

ww.Audio recordings made on a phone or a mi: Audio recordings have no fixed table layout and are unstructured data, so they do not fit the definition of structured data.
ww.Free-form text such as emails and notes: Free-form text such as emails and notes has no fixed fields, which makes it unstructured and not structured.
ww.Photos and videos taken with a phone or: Photos and videos are stored as pixel or frame data with no table of fields, so they are unstructured.

rw: Unstructured data has no predefined format or fixed fields, as with images, audio and free text, so it needs special methods to analyze.

ww.Rows in a table arranged in a fixed set: Rows with a fixed set of columns and labels describe structured data, which is the opposite of unstructured data that lacks a fixed layout.
ww.A spreadsheet that holds numbers and tex: A spreadsheet with labeled cells and rows has a clear structure, so it is structured data and not unstructured.
ww.A SQL table that stores each record in a: A SQL table stores records in a fixed layout of rows and columns, which is the definition of structured data, not unstructured.

rw: Semi-structured data has some organization, such as tags or key-value pairs, but no rigid table, and JSON and XML files are common examples.

ww.A strict database table with fixed rows: A strict table with fixed rows, columns and set types is fully structured, so it is not semi-structured, which lacks a rigid layout.
ww.A plain image file such as a photo or a: A plain image with no data fields is unstructured, and semi-structured data has tags or keys that give it some organization.
ww.A random guess made by an analyst about: A guess made without checking is an assumption and not a type of data, so it has no link to semi-structured data.

rw: A categorical variable represents a label or group, such as color or city, and its values name categories and are not measured amounts.

ww.A date only, with no other detail: A date is only one possible kind of value, so saying a categorical variable is a date only is far too narrow and wrong.
ww.A calculation result such as a total: A calculation result such as a total is a number, which is numerical and not a category label.
ww.A measurable amount in a data table: A measurable amount is a numerical variable, whereas a categorical variable names a group or label, so this describes the other type.

rw: A numerical variable represents a quantity that can be measured or counted, such as height, price or number of students, and supports arithmetic.

ww.A group name or a category label in data: A group name or category label is a categorical variable, not numerical, since numerical variables hold quantities that can be measured or counted.
ww.A color name such as red or blue in a co: A color name such as red or blue is a category label, which makes it categorical and not a numerical quantity.
ww.A text label for each record in the tabl: A text label for each record names or describes it and is categorical, so it does not represent a measured quantity.

rw: The number of students is counted in whole numbers and cannot be fractional, so it takes separate values and is a discrete variable.

ww.Temperature in degrees now: Temperature can take any value in a range, including decimals, so it is continuous and not a discrete variable.
ww.Height of a student on a scale: Height can take any value within a range, such as 150.3 cm, so it is a continuous variable and not discrete.
ww.Time to run a mile in minutes: Time to run a mile can be any value in minutes, including fractions, so it is continuous and not discrete.

rw: Weight of a package can take any value within a range, including fractions, so it is measured and not counted, which makes it continuous.

ww.Number of pets owned: The number of pets owned is counted in whole numbers, so it is a discrete variable and not continuous.
ww.Siblings in the home: Siblings in the home are counted as whole numbers, so this is a discrete variable, since nobody has 1.5 siblings.
ww.Number of cars owned: The number of cars owned is a count in whole numbers, so it is discrete and not a continuous variable.

rw: An ordinal variable is a category with a meaningful order, such as small, medium and large, though the gaps between levels are not exactly equal.

ww.A date shown as day, month and year in a: A date shown as day, month and year describes a point in time, which is not an ordered category, so this is not an ordinal variable.
ww.A number with equal spacing such as a me: A number with equal spacing such as weight or height is a measured quantity and so is numerical, not ordinal, which is a ranked category.
ww.A random label given to each item with n: A random label with no order is a nominal category, and ordinal data require a meaningful order, so this does not fit.

rw: A boolean type holds one of two values, true or false, which makes it useful for yes or no flags and conditions in code and data.

ww.A date and time stamp value: A date and time stamp records a moment and is a datetime type, so it does not hold just a true or false value.
ww.A decimal number such as 3.14: A decimal number such as 3.14 is a float type, which holds numeric values, so it is different from a boolean with two states.
ww.A word or a text value in a cell: A word or text value is a string type, so it is a different data type from a boolean that holds only true or false.

rw: A string is a sequence of characters, such as letters, digits and symbols, used to store text like names and messages in a program.

ww.A true or false value: A true or false value is a boolean, which holds only two states, whereas a string holds a sequence of characters.
ww.A whole number value: A whole number value is an integer type and holds counts and not text, so it is not a string.
ww.A decimal number value: A decimal number value is a float type used for numbers with fractions, so it is not a string, which holds text.

rw: Metadata is data that describes other data, such as a file's author, date created, size or format, which helps people find and understand it.

ww.A backup copy of all the data: A backup copy is a duplicate of the data kept for recovery, so it is not metadata, which describes the data and does not copy it.
ww.Raw measurements from sensors: Raw measurements from sensors are primary data and not metadata, which gives information about data such as its source, time or format.
ww.A graph of the results of data: A graph of the results is a visualization of data, so it is not metadata, which describes other data and does not display it.

rw: Primary data are collected directly by the researcher for a specific purpose, such as through a survey, interview or experiment, so the collector controls how it is gathered.

ww.A textbook or library copy of the data u: A textbook or library copy was gathered earlier by other people, so it is a secondary source and not primary data.
ww.Data from an old report written by other: Data from an old report written by others was collected by someone else, which makes it secondary and not primary.
ww.Data copied from a website and cleaned b: Data copied from a website was collected earlier by someone else, so even after cleaning it is secondary and not primary.

rw: Secondary data were originally collected by someone else for another purpose, such as published reports or public datasets, and are reused for new analysis.

ww.A survey you design and run yourself: A survey you design and run yourself is primary data, since you collect it directly, so it is not a secondary source.
ww.Interviews you conduct yourself with cus: Interviews you conduct yourself are collected first-hand, which makes them primary data and not secondary.
ww.An experiment you run on your own team: An experiment you run on your own team produces first-hand data, so it is a primary source and not secondary.

rw: The 100 students surveyed are a subset drawn from the 2,000 students at the school, which makes them a sample of the population.

ww.Parameter: A parameter is a value describing a whole population, such as its mean, and not the group of students surveyed, so it does not name them.
ww.A census: A census would survey all 2,000 students, but only 100 were surveyed, so this group is a sample and not a census.
ww.Population: The population is all 2,000 students at the school, and the 100 surveyed are only a part of that group.

rw: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected, which helps the sample represent the whole group fairly.

ww.Picking volunteers only, who sign up on: Volunteers who sign up on their own are a self-selected group, which is not random and can bias results.
ww.Picking friends and family of the resear: Friends and family of the researcher are chosen for convenience and are not an equal-chance selection, so this is not random sampling.
ww.Picking the easiest people to reach and: Picking the easiest people to reach is convenience sampling, which gives some people no chance of being chosen, so it is not random.

rw: Surveying only cafeteria students leaves out students who eat elsewhere, so the sample is unrepresentative, which is sampling bias.

ww.Perfect sample: A sample missing students who eat elsewhere is not perfect, because it does not represent all students, so calling it perfect is wrong.
ww.A larger sample: The problem is who is included, not how many, so a larger sample drawn the same way would keep the same bias.
ww.No problem: Surveying only cafeteria students leaves out other students, so there is a clear problem, and the claim of no problem ignores it.

rw: A stratified sample draws from each subgroup in proportion to its size, so each group is fairly represented in the final sample.

ww.A sample of only volunteers, who sign up: A sample of only volunteers is self-selected and does not reflect the subgroups of the population in proportion, so it is not stratified.
ww.A sample of one person picked by the res: A single person picked by the researcher is far too small and not drawn from each subgroup, so it is not a stratified sample.
ww.A sample from one class in the school, p: A sample from one class at one school covers just one group and ignores the others, so it is not stratified.

rw: A census surveys every member of a population instead of just a sample, giving complete data but usually at higher cost and effort.

ww.A random guess about the size of a popul: A guess about the size of a population is an estimate and not a count, while a census collects data from every member.
ww.A chart of the results of a poll in a to: A chart of poll results shows data and is not a way of collecting it, whereas a census is a survey of everyone.
ww.A survey of a sample drawn at random her: A survey of a random sample covers only part of the population, so it is a sample survey and not a census.

rw: A leading question is worded to push respondents toward a particular answer, which biases the results and makes them less reliable.

ww.A neutral question worded so that it fav: A neutral question favors no answer, which is the opposite of a leading question, so it cannot be the one that pushes respondents.
ww.A short question that takes only a few s: A short question is not leading because of its length, since wording that steers the answer is what makes a question leading.
ww.A multiple-choice question that has seve: Listing several answers is the multiple-choice format and says nothing about steering respondents, so it does not make a question leading.

rw: Response bias occurs when respondents give inaccurate answers because of wording, social pressure or the wish to please, which distorts the survey results.

ww.A perfect survey in which every answer i: A survey where every answer is true and carefully given would have no response bias, so this describes the absence of the problem.
ww.A random error that occurs by chance and: A random error occurs by chance with no pattern, but response bias follows a pattern, so these are different kinds of survey error.
ww.A sampling rule that decides which peopl: A sampling rule decides who is asked, which concerns sampling and not how people answer, so it is not response bias.

rw: The mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values, so it is the usual average and uses every value.

ww.The middle value in the sorted data set: The middle value in sorted data is the median, so this is a different measure of center from the mean.
ww.The largest value in the data set of num: The largest value is the maximum, which is not a measure of center, so it is not the mean of the data.
ww.The most common value in the data set of: The most common value is the mode, so this is a different measure from the mean, which uses every value.

rw: The sum is 4+8+6+10+12 = 40, and dividing by the 5 values gives a mean of 8.

ww.6: The mean is the sum divided by the count, so 4+8+6+10+12 = 40 and 40/5 = 8, which means 6 is not the mean.
ww.10: Ten is the largest number but the mean is 40/5 = 8, so ten overstates the average.
ww.40: Forty is the sum of the values and not the mean, because the sum must still be divided by 5 values to give 8.

rw: Sorted, the values are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and with five values the third, 7, is the middle, so the median is 7.

ww.5: Sorted, the values are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and the middle is 7, so 5 is only the second value and not the median.
ww.9: Nine is the fourth of the five sorted values 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, so it is not the middle, since the third value, 7, is.
ww.7.5: With five values there is a single middle one, 7, and no averaging of two values is needed, so 7.5 is wrong.

rw: With four values the median is the average of the two middle ones, so (4+6)/2 = 10/2 = 5.

ww.4: Sorted values 2, 4, 6, 8 have two middle values, 4 and 6, so the median is their average, 5, and 4 is only one of them.
ww.6: Six is the third value and only one of the two middle values, and the median is (4+6)/2 = 5, not 6.
ww.20: Twenty is the sum of 2+4+6+8, not the median, and the median is the average of the two middle values, 4 and 6, giving 5.

rw: The mode is the value that occurs most often in a data set, and a set can have one mode, several modes or none.

ww.The smallest value in the data set: The smallest value is the minimum and has nothing to do with how often a value occurs, which is what the mode measures.
ww.The average of all the values: The average of all the values is the mean, which is a different measure of center from the mode.
ww.The middle value of the data: The middle value of the data is the median, so this is a different measure from the mode, which counts frequency.

rw: Three appears three times in the list, more often than any other value, so the mode is 3.

ww.4: Four appears once, while 3 appears three times, so 4 is not the most frequent value and cannot be the mode.
ww.6: Six appears once in 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 3, 6, while 3 appears three times, so 6 is not the most common value.
ww.3.7: Thirty-seven tenths is not even a value in the list, and the mode must be a value that occurs, so 3.7 cannot be the mode.

rw: The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values, giving a simple measure of how far apart the extremes in the data are.

ww.The average of all of the values in the: The average of all values is the mean, which measures center and not spread, so it is not the range.
ww.The middle value when the data are put i: The middle value in order is the median, a measure of center, while the range measures the full spread of the data.
ww.The most common value in the data set of: The most common value is the mode, which is a different measure from the range, and it does not describe spread.

rw: The largest value is 20 and the smallest is 7, so the range is 20 - 7 = 13.

ww.7: Seven is the smallest value and not the range, which needs the smallest subtracted from the largest, 20 - 7 = 13.
ww.20: Twenty is the largest value alone, and the range subtracts the smallest, 7, from it, giving 20 - 7 = 13.
ww.12.6: About 12.6 is the mean of the values (12+7+20+15+9 = 63, and 63/5 = 12.6), not the range, which is max minus min.

rw: The median depends only on the middle position in sorted data, so an extreme outlier barely changes it, which makes it the least affected measure.

ww.The sum: The sum includes every value, so one extreme outlier changes it greatly, which makes it very sensitive to outliers.
ww.The mean: The mean uses every value, so a single extreme outlier pulls it toward the outlier, which makes it sensitive to extremes.
ww.The range: The range is the largest value minus the smallest, so an outlier directly changes it, and it is highly sensitive to extremes.

rw: Variance is the average of the squared differences from the mean, which measures how spread out the values are in squared units.

ww.The middle value after the data are put: The middle value after ordering is the median, a measure of center, so it does not describe variance, which measures spread.
ww.The sum of the values divided by their c: The sum divided by the count is the mean, which is a measure of center, so it is a different measure from variance.
ww.The largest value minus the smallest val: The largest minus the smallest value is the range, a simpler spread measure that uses only two values, whereas variance uses all values.

rw: Quartiles are the three values Q1, Q2 and Q3 that split ordered data into four equal parts, each holding about 25% of the data.

ww.A type of chart that shows data as bars,: A type of chart showing bars, lines or slices is a graph type, not a quartile, which is a value that divides ordered data.
ww.A type of mean found by adding the value: A type of mean found by adding and dividing describes an average, which is a different idea from quartiles that split the data into parts.
ww.A type of outlier that is far above or f: An outlier is a value far from the rest, and a quartile is a dividing point of the data, so these are different ideas.

rw: The IQR is Q3 minus Q1, which gives the spread of the middle 50% of the data and resists the effect of outliers.

ww.Max minus min: Max minus min is the range, which uses only the two extreme values, and the IQR uses the quartiles instead.
ww.The mean: The mean is the average of all values, a measure of center, so it is not the IQR, which measures the spread of the middle half.
ww.Q1 plus Q3: Adding Q1 and Q3 gives a sum with no meaning as a spread, whereas the IQR is found by subtracting Q1 from Q3.

rw: A box plot displays the median, the quartiles and potential outliers, giving a compact picture of the spread and center of the data.

ww.Only the total of all the values in the: A box plot does not show only the total of the values, since it displays the median, quartiles and outliers, and not a sum.
ww.Only the mode, the value that appears mo: A box plot does not show only the mode, because it summarizes the median, quartiles and outliers, not the most frequent value.
ww.Only the mean, the sum of the values div: A box plot does not show only the mean, because it displays the median, quartiles and potential outliers of the data.

rw: A histogram is a bar chart showing the frequency of values in ranges, called bins, which reveals the shape of the distribution.

ww.A pie chart showing shares of a whole as: A pie chart shows shares of a whole as slices, whereas a histogram shows how many values fall in each range of a numeric variable.
ww.A line of best fit drawn through the poi: A line of best fit is drawn on a scatter plot to show a trend, which is a different tool from a histogram.
ww.A scatter of two variables plotted again: A scatter of two variables plotted against each other is a scatter plot and shows a relationship, whereas a histogram shows one variable.

rw: By the empirical rule, about 68% of the data in a normal distribution lies within one standard deviation of the mean.

ww.99.7%: About 99.7% lies within three standard deviations of the mean, so this figure is for a wider interval than one deviation.
ww.95%: About 95% lies within two standard deviations, not one, so this figure belongs to a wider interval than the one asked about.
ww.50%: Fifty percent is the share on each side of the mean and not the share within one standard deviation, which is about 68%.

rw: By the empirical rule, about 95% of the data in a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean.

ww.68%: About 68% lies within one standard deviation, not two, so this figure is too low for the interval asked about.
ww.75%: Seventy-five percent is not a value from the empirical rule, which gives 68%, 95% and 99.7% for one, two and three deviations.
ww.99.7%: About 99.7% lies within three standard deviations, so this is the figure for three and not for two.

rw: Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution, showing whether it has a longer tail on the right or on the left.

ww.A measure of size for a set of data valu: Size is measured by count or by total, and skewness is a measure of the shape of a distribution, not its size.
ww.A measure of spread around the mean of d: Spread around the mean is measured by variance and standard deviation, while skewness describes how lopsided the distribution is.
ww.A measure of center for a set of data va: Center is measured by the mean, median or mode, and skewness is a different measure that describes the shape of a distribution.

rw: A long tail to the right is right skewed, also called positively skewed, with the mean usually pulled above the median.

ww.Uniform in shape overall: A uniform distribution has roughly equal frequency across values and no long tail, so it does not match a long right tail.
ww.Symmetric in shape overall: A symmetric distribution looks the same on both sides of the center, and a long right tail makes it lopsided, so it is not symmetric.
ww.Left skewed, long left tail: A left skewed distribution has its long tail on the left, but this one has its long tail on the right, so it is not left skewed.
